newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW-GM seeks Euro gains with new Astra.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-GM seeks Euro gains with new Astra.

text.p: General Motors Corp, the world's biggest carmaker, is counting on an overhaul of its popular Astra model to be unveiled next month to boost sagging European sales and help ignite demand in emerging markets.

Louis Hughes, the executive in charge of GM's international operations, said on Friday that the U.S. carmaker has plans for 1998 annual global production of about 800,000 vehicles based on the Astra platform at plants in Europe and Brazil.
That's up from European Astra model production of about 560,000 vehicles in 1996.
It is also expected that the new Astra models will carry a 12-year rust guarantee to match one to be offered by rival carmaker Volkswagen AG with its new Golf model.
The new Astra models will be unveiled at the Frankfurt car show in September and will be available for European delivery in the spring of 1998 under the Opel and Vauxhall brands.
"I do not think our situation is unique," Hughes said of GM's decline so far in 1997 in European market share as well as the decline in 1996 to 12.5 percent from 13.1 percent in 1995.

"The fact is that when we get the new Astra models up and running, we certainly expect an increase in market share. I see it as a temporary period created by the changeover cycle," he said in the interview at GM's international unit headquarters.
Hughes said GM was producing as many as possible of the compact Astras, a top competitor to the VW Golf, ahead of the changeover.
He also said GM's German-based Opel and Britain-based Vauxhall units were currently strained on capacity for many of their models, particularly the hot-selling subcompact Corsa.

"The only reason that we are losing any market share is that we are strained on capacity with the Corsa and we are in the run-out phase of the Astra," Hughes said, noting GM has consistently been the most efficient European carmaker.
Hughes said GM was considering whether to reduce exports of Corsa models made at its plant in Eisenach, Germany, which Opel officials say is running at virtually 100 percent capacity.

With the planned opening of a new factory in Argentina, GM can build about one million Corsas a year at 11 plants in 10 countries and sell the car at what Hughes calls "a very nice profit" in about 75 countries.
"We are thinking about selling Corsas made in Europe in the region rather than exporting them and let some of these other plants fill export needs," Hughes said.
"It is one of the additional advantage of going to the same Opel product around the world," he said.

But Hughes is also counting on the Astra, and particularly the Zafira compact van due out in late 1998 that will be based on the Astra platform, to help put GM back in the hunt to catch up with the VW brands that also include SEAT, Audi and Skoda.

"I think what really comes across is that the Astra styling is very dynamic," he said. "It is not an evolutionary styling, as you can see from some of our competitors. You see the tension in the sheet metal on purpose to give it a much more sportier feel."
Hughes said market research showed potential customers would be willing to pay about 40,000 marks for the car, far more than the roughly 24,000 marks price of the current model.
The new Astra would in fact be priced close to current model, Hughes said.
The new Zafira model will also break new ground, Hughes says, since it can seat up to seven people and will be one of the first models in this market segment.

GM officials in particular see no threat to the vehicle from the Mercedes A-class developed by Germany's Daimler-Benz AG because the Zafira can accommodate more passengers and is more functional for about the same price.
Hughes said he saw a good chance for volume growth in the compact van segment, unlike for mini-vans which he said were a "niche market" where partnerships are required to make profit.
